newsitem.title: GERMANY: German police brace for clashes on Hess anniversary.
newsitem.headline: German police brace for clashes on Hess anniversary.

text.p: Police across Germany are bracing for clashes with neo-Nazi groups this weekend on the 10th anniversary of the death of Hitler's deputy, Rudolf Hess.

Hess hanged himself with an electric cord in Berlin's Spandau prison on August 17, 1987, and the date has become a rallying point for the radical right in Germany and other European countries in recent years.
German police detained 160 right-wing activists on the ninth anniversary last year, while hundreds of neo-Nazis battled with police in Sweden, Norway and Denmark.

"Hess has become a martyr figure for the neo-Nazis," said Hans-Gert Lange, spokesman for the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), which tracks activities of far-right groups and has penetrated them with informants.
"Hess has become a symbol that excites them. It is a chance to try to fool the police and hold their rallies," he said.

A senior official in the eastern state of Saxony said his authorities had slapped a general ban on any rallies connected to the anniversary. Neo-Nazi violence in eastern Germany shot up after the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989.
Saxony Interior Minister Klaus Hardraht said police would not tolerate any violation of the ban and were in a position to deal with any neo-Nazi activity.
But thousands of extremists across Germany will try to defy police bans and stage rallies at secret locations to celebrate the 10th anniversary of Hess's death.

Hess, the private secretary to whom Hitler dictated his political testament Mein Kampf, became deputy Fuehrer in 1932. He was effectively in charge of the Nazi party until 1941, when he parachuted into Scotland on a mysterious mission to press for an Anglo-German alliance against the Soviet Union.
He spent the rest of his life in custody, the last two decades as the sole inmate of Spandau where, many extremists claim, he was murdered by the Allies.
In Germany, attention-grabbing acts by right-wing extremists are widely reported. They tend to cause intense disquiet in a country still haunted by the Nazi era.
But authorities say the menace is confined to a small and disparate, if dangerous, collection of rabble-rousers.
The BfV estimates there are about 6,500 militant right-wing extremists among Germany's 82 million people.

Aside from the hard-core fanatics, who authorities say have no compunction about resorting to violence against foreigners or any other perceived enemies, police believe another 35,000 Nazi sympathisers are active in far-right groups.
"The number of right-wing extremists is, in comparison to the population, negligibly small," said Lange.
"They pose no threat to the constitution. They are not organised in any real sense of the word -- rather, they are often misguided individuals who act spontaneously.

"But for obvious reasons, Germans are extremely sensitive to the far right," he added. "There are roughly the same number of left-wing extremists, but they don't generate anywhere near the same level of alarm."
Alarm bells invariably go off when right-wing extremists are implicated, as in recent months, in firebombings of churches or centres for asylum-seekers.
Newspapers often carry articles about swastikas being daubed on Jewish gravestones, or acts of xenophobia.

Last week, two young German army soldiers were discharged for firebombing a hostel for foreign workers in the eastern city of Dresden. The soldiers, who were caught after witnesses saw them shouting Nazi slogans near the fire, admitted their motive was hatred of foreigners. No one was hurt.

"Every attack on an asylum home or on a bus with people shouting 'Sieg Heil' is one attack too many," said Andreas Nachama, head of the Jewish Community in Berlin. "You can see these attacks all over Germany and even in churches. It is a cancerous disease that has spread and we will not tolerate it."

Right-wing extremism was all but been eradicated from West Germany in the four decades following World War Two, but the genie escaped from the bottle again after the collapse of the Berlin Wall that led to unification with East Germany.

A tide of racist attacks surged in the former communist east and spread westwards. The number of acts of right-wing violence exploded from fewer than 200 a year in the 1980s to 2,639 at its peak in 1992, when six people were killed.

Fourteen more died between 1990 and 1993, and dozens were hurt in cases of attempted murder. The government cracked down hard, if belatedly, and the number of attacks fell to 781 in 1996, when one person was killed.

"The state has the far-right as a group largely under control at the moment," said Gabriele Nandlinger, an editor at the Blick Nach Rechts newsletter that tracks the extremists. "But they are unable to stop the individual acts of violence."
